# Wisdom Calls Out: The Enduring Relevance of Proverbs

Proverbs is timely and timeless—a treasure trove for disciple and church leader, father and mother, youth and adult, world citizen and civic ruler. Across ages, eras, and cultures, Proverbs proves the relevance and superiority of God's wisdom. It unashamedly asserts that this is God's world and those who rightly order their lives after God's design will best navigate the complexity of this fallen cosmos with a well-lived life. As we read "the proverbs of Solomon" (1:1) given to his son, we find ourselves among his audience, eager to obtain a life of wisdom. Proverbs is God's inspired word to help us live wisely in God's world—to faithfully trek through the current world and to joyfully enter into the world to come, world without end. Proverbs addresses both our temporal earthly existence and unending eternal bliss. Although an ancient text, "wisdom calls out" (1:20) to us as it was calling out to Solomon's son in his day.

The book of Proverbs orients us to the life of faith as moral formation in the fear of God (1:7). It depicts the life of faith as a journey toward wisdom—urging us to choose the path of righteousness, forsake the way of evil, and learn to walk prudently in God's world. Importantly, this piece of wisdom literature offers vivid, side-by-side portraits of godly manhood and virtuous womanhood. These portraits inspire the young to emulate godliness put on display by trustworthy exemplars. It also inspires this godly emulation with warnings depicted by godless examples—the self-destructive gang, the self-corrupting evil man, and the self-ensnaring wayward woman. But one of Proverbs great features is that it also outlines pathways for crossing thresholds from naive youth to mature adulthood. Part of Proverbs genius is its divine guidance on how to move—make passage—from naivete and simplicity to wisdom and prudence.

Solomon had to prepare his son for a dangerous world—a menacing cosmos filled with hazard to heart and home. His son would occupy a throne, so he needed his personal life to have a nobility that matched the dignity and significance of his royal throne. But the path to nobility and royalty is lined with obstacle, foe, and hazard. The world in Solomon's day is not too different from our own. Voices clamor for our attention, seeking to undermine personal faith and household integrity. Society and faith community are more assaulted by false belief and errant ideology than sword or bomb. Dark enemies lurk, tempting us to moral compromise, foolish living, and childish fancy all in the name of pleasure-seeking. Foolishness adorns itself with an attractive exterior. Evil parades under the banner of human progress. Lust endears itself to humanity with empty promises of immediate gratification. The enemy seeks to lead youth, simple, and foolish off a precipice of our own making. Proverbs clearly shows that the path to death and destruction is lined with glittering vice.

The book of Proverbs assists us in navigating a world fraught with subtle and hostile enemies. Solomon's counsel beckons us to wisdom in the fear of God. But Solomon was not only interested in raising a son who would embody wisdom. He wanted his son to grow up to be a man who would deploy his faith—a faith formed in the fear of God—into the world to enact wisdom in society on behalf of God. Solomon wanted his son to grow up to be regal agent who would transformed the disordered world and reclaim it for righteousness, reorder it after God's design, and render it subservient to Christ. He also wanted young women to forsake the life of the wayward harlot and to embrace the nobility of the virtuous woman. Even in the sphere of Christianity, we can suffer from an androgynous spirituality: generic applications to Christian living without regard to the specific scriptural injunctions to men and women. That Proverbs offers biblical portraits of godly men and godly women, helps young disciples—male and female—learn their specific role in being redemptive agents in the world.

The following is a primer on the book of Proverbs. It explores the relationship between the pursuit of wisdom and the nature of faith formation, discerning the underling spiritual pedagogy outlined in Proverbs 1-9. It investigates the root metaphor of journey and quest, and its importance to spiritual growth. It wrestles through the idea of rites of passage, particularly harvesting this idea from Solomon's initial lectures in Proverbs 1-9. It also discusses the nature of biblical masculinity as depicted in Proverbs.

## Key Ideas

- Proverbs provides timely and timeless wisdom for God's people.
- The picture of mature faith in Proverbs is the pursuit of wisdom in the fear of God—the fear of the Lord is a synonym of faith.
- Wisdom education seeks to train people how to rightly live in God's world, which is currently dangerous and deadly because of the results of sin.

## Reflection Questions

<Question id="Pro-Ses2-RefQue-1">1. What kind of wisdom do you live by? Are you pursuing a life of wisdom?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses2-RefQue-2">2. As you consider what it means to be a Christian, how important is it to gain true wisdom?</Question>
<Question id="Pro-Ses2-RefQue-3">3. How can gaining biblical wisdom help us navigate the complexities of the fallen world in which we live?</Question>
